candidates.label: Areopagus Hill
candidates.support: A rocky outcrop northwest of the Acropolis, named for a mythical trial of the god Ares; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places the Court of the Areopagus in this same neighborhood, next to the Painted Portico where Paul had been disputing with Stoic philosophers, and the hill is traditionally identified as the setting of Paul's speech in Acts 17. Wikidata's coordinate for the hill is corroborated by an independently maintained gazetteer of ancient places, which likewise marks it northwest of the Acropolis.

summary.text: The Areopagus ("Hill of Ares") is a rocky outcrop in Athens, northwest of the Acropolis, which gave its name to an ancient council that met there and that also sat in judgment on serious cases. According to Acts, the Athenians brought Paul to the Areopagus to explain his teaching about Jesus and the resurrection, and there he preached about an altar he had seen inscribed "TO AN UNKNOWN GOD."

history.text: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places the Court of the Areopagus near the Painted Portico (Stoa Poecile), where Paul had been reasoning daily with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers in the marketplace below, and notes that the philosopher Socrates had faced his own accusers in the same neighborhood five centuries before Paul.

Acts records that when Paul spoke of the resurrection of the dead, some of his hearers mocked him, but others wanted to hear more, and a few believed, including a member of the council named Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris.

scripture.textWEB: They took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is, which you are speaking about?
Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and said, “You men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things.

politicalHistory.note: The Roman biographer Suetonius: on his departure from Greece, the emperor Nero "presented the entire province with freedom."

The Roman biographer Suetonius records that the emperor Vespasian "made provinces of Achaia, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium and Samos, taking away their freedom," but gives no year for this, so the status here is shown as unclear from Vespasian's first full year as emperor until his death in 79, when it is a province again.
